findings.headline: Strategic asset disposal programme following prior debt warning from MHCLG
findings.detail: The council received a non-statutory Best Value Notice flagging high debt levels and placed a moratorium on new investment debt. Ahead of Local Government Reorganisation into West Surrey authority, the council is now pursuing strategic disposals of underperforming assets, with reduction of borrowing identified as a key strategic focus. The paper explicitly states this may necessitate selling commercial assets to alleviate borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Prior regulatory flagging for high debt followed by forced asset sales indicates the council was pushed to address debt levels and is shedding assets to restore financial stability.
findings.figures: Non-statutory Best Value Notice received; debt moratorium placed
findings.quote: A key strategic focus for the property team moving forward will be the reduction of borrowing and the long-term liabilities associated with managing a large commercial portfolio. This may necessitate the disposal of certain commercial assets to alleviate borrowing costs and improve financial resilience.

findings.headline: Quarterly vacancy loss of £603,848 with multiple assets unlet
findings.detail: In Q4 2026, the investment portfolio generated £603,848 in lost income through vacancy. Properties remaining unlet include Osprey House, floors in Pine Trees Estate, units in Addlestone One and Magna Square, Charter Place, The Precinct, and units in Addlestone. The assets team is actively marketing but has not yet converted interest into leases.
findings.matters: Prolonged vacancies reduce revenue whilst the council continues to carry debt servicing and holding costs, eroding returns and income certainty.
findings.figures: £603,848 income loss through vacancy in Q4
findings.quote: the total loss of income in the investment portfolio through vacancy in Q4 is £603,848. Some of our vacant properties include: Osprey House, Grnd & 1st floor Building 5 Pine Trees, Units in Addlestone One and Magna Square

findings.headline: Portfolio heavily concentrated in office sector experiencing sharp value declines
findings.detail: The council holds 31 investment properties heavily weighted to office assets. Major office holdings are experiencing significant losses: Pine Trees Estate fell from £80.7m to £36.56m, 610 Chiswick High Road fell from £65.1m to £32.9m, Honeywell House fell from £32m to £11.9m. The portfolio lacks diversification, making it vulnerable to continued office market weakness.
findings.matters: Concentrated exposure to a declining asset class increases portfolio risk and limits income resilience if office sector conditions deteriorate further.
findings.figures: Pine Trees £80.7m purchase, £36.56m valuation; 610 Chiswick £65.1m purchase, £32.9m valuation; Honeywell House £31.96m purchase, £11.9m valuation
findings.quote: the portfolio is heavily weighted to offices by both number of properties and capital value, this shows the portfolio is not a traditionally balanced portfolio so is much more susceptible to changes within the office sector than a balanced portfolio might be.

findings.headline: Cumulative capital losses of £177.5m across the portfolio since purchase
findings.detail: The valuation as at 31 March 2026 shows accumulated capital appreciation/reduction of negative £177.49m, compared to negative £166.58m the prior year. The annual decline alone was £10.9m, more than double the prior year's £3.85m decline, indicating accelerating deterioration.
findings.matters: Large unrealised losses indicate the portfolio is generating negative returns on deployment and constrains the council's financial flexibility and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £-177,493,823 (Previous year £-166,583,823); Annual decline £-10,910,000 (Previous year £-3,847,500)
findings.quote: Difference in Capital Values, since purchase £-177,493,823 (Previous year £-166,583,823)

findings.headline: Loan-to-Value ratio of 137% shows debt now exceeds asset value
findings.detail: The council's LTV ratio has deteriorated from 133% in the prior year to 137% in Q4 2025/26. This means the total debt owed on the investment property portfolio exceeds the current market value of those properties, representing a critical erosion of loan coverage.
findings.matters: Lenders use LTV as a primary credit metric; a ratio above 100% indicates negative equity and that the borrower has insufficient asset backing for outstanding debt.
findings.figures: 137% (Previous Year – 133%)
findings.quote: A figure of over 100% shows that the value of the assets have fallen below the amounts borrowed.

findings.headline: Council repaid £10m PWLB loan from cash reserves rather than refinancing, accepting liquidity risk to avoid 5%+ borrowing costs.
findings.detail: A £10m PWLB loan maturing August 2025 was repaid using internal cash (known as internal borrowing) because long-term PWLB rates exceeded 5% while short-term investment returns were equal or superior. This strategy depends on interest rate forecasts falling to avoid a refinancing cost penalty, and assumes adequate cash buffers remain available for operational needs.
findings.matters: A lender assesses liquidity management and whether the council is maintaining prudent reserves. Using cash balances to avoid borrowing is a bet on future rates; if rates rise or unexpected demands consume reserves, the council faces expensive emergency refinancing.
findings.figures: £10.0m PWLB loan repaid August 2025 at rates 'greater than 5%'; closing investments £78.3m
findings.quote: The Council has repaid a £10.0m PWLB loan that matured in August 2025.  In view of the high-interest rate environment (greater than 5%), this was repaid using existing cash resources to temporarily fill the gap (known as internal borrowing)

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme delivered at only 23% of budget; £6.1m of planned investment unexecuted.
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure was £1,856k against a budget of £7,986k, a 77% underspend. This represents a deterioration from 2024/25 when spend was £2,910k. The HRA fared better at 67% execution (£15,235k of £22,763k), but General Fund slippage suggests delivery challenges or material unplanned de-scoping.
findings.matters: Large capital underspend indicates weak project delivery, deferred investment in service assets, or financial stress. A lender evaluates capital discipline and whether the council can execute its financial and strategic plans.
findings.figures: General Fund: Budget £7,986k, Actual £1,856k (23% execution); HRA: Budget £22,763k, Actual £15,235k (67% execution)
findings.quote: The actual capital expenditure forms one of the required prudential indicators.  The table below shows the actual capital expenditure and how this was financed

findings.headline: Wholly-owned subsidiary company RBC Investments Ltd has defaulted on interest payments totalling £309,000.
findings.detail: RBC Investments Ltd failed to make scheduled interest payments due 03 July 2025 and 03 January 2026, both now outstanding. The council holds £41.9m in loans across three wholly-owned companies. A March 2025 report flagged repayment issues and triggered refinancing investigations, but resolution has stalled: officers describe progress as 'slower than anticipated' and remain 'in the final process of stage two' of agreed actions.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether subsidiary investments pose credit risk or balance-sheet loss. £41.9m of loans to companies unable to service debt raises questions about underlying viability, whether principal is recoverable, and whether the council faces future write-downs.
findings.figures: £309,000 missed interest payments; £41,909k total loans to subsidiaries (RBC Investments Ltd: £38,409k)
findings.quote: RBC Investments Ltd did not make the scheduled interest payments of £309,000 on 03 July 2025 or on 03 January and this balance remains outstanding

findings.headline: Housing repairs contractor has consistently failed to meet performance targets despite two formal Improvement Notices (October 2023, August 2024)
findings.detail: The five-year responsive repairs and voids contract commenced April 2023. Despite monthly reporting against performance targets, the contractor has failed consistently to meet them, prompting Improvement Notices in October 2023 and again in August 2024. Work orders are not being completed within assigned timeframes and quality inspections are not always completed timely.
findings.matters: Persistent contractor failure to meet repair targets suggests either inadequate service delivery, cost pressures from remedial/rework, or poor contract management; two improvement notices in two years indicates the problem is not being resolved.
findings.figures: Five-year contract commenced April 2023, Improvement Notices October 2023 and August 2024
findings.quote: The Council has contracted out the responsive repair and void services for a five-year term which commenced in April 2023. The contract agreement includes performance indicators which sets agreed targets for the contractor to meet and are reported every month, however, due to consistent failure of the contractor to meet these targets, two 'Improvement Notices' have been issued (October 2023 and August 2024)

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued a C4 rating ("very serious failings") in February 2026, requiring fundamental changes to council's housing delivery
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing concluded in February 2026 that the council has very serious failings in delivering outcomes of the consumer standards and serious failings in delivering the Rent Standard. The council had self-referred a historic rent-setting issue prior to the inspection. The council is now establishing improvement plans to address the fundamental failures.
findings.matters: A C4 rating signals breakdown in a major council service; the self-referred rent-setting issue indicates prior non-compliance with rent regulations, suggesting potential financial exposure and questions over the adequacy of housing finance controls.
findings.figures: C4 rating issued February 2026, self-referred historic rent setting issue
findings.quote: The Regulators report and judgement was issued in February 2026, concluding a C4 rating (Consumer) - Our judgement is that there are very serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards. The landlord must make fundamental changes so that improved outcomes are delivered. The Regulator also concluded that there are serious failings in how the Council is delivering the outcomes of the Rent Standard.

findings.headline: Fire safety follow-up actions are systematically incomplete with 294 overdue and no documented progress on 281 of them; a lift inspection was missed resulting in a 16-month gap
findings.detail: The council's fire safety action tracking system is failing: 294 fire follow-up actions have not been completed within the specified timeframe and 281 of these have no recorded comments on progress. Separately, a passenger lift inspection was missed, creating a 16-month gap between inspections. The electrical safety inspection contract expired on 1 July 2024 and the council continues work without a renewed contract, with no evidence provided of coverage for the July-December 2024 period.
findings.matters: A 16-month gap in lift inspections is a serious health and safety breach; 294 overdue fire actions with no tracking suggests systemic loss of control over a critical function. This creates liability exposure and indicates the council's safety compliance infrastructure is broken.
findings.figures: 294 follow up actions overdue, 281 with no progress comments, 59 overdue inspections (fire), 16-month delay on lift inspection, electrical safety contract expired 1 July 2024
findings.quote: We noted that 294 follow up actions (fire) had not been completed within the specified timeframe, and of these 281 had no comments to confirm that progress towards these actions had taken place. We also noted 59 overdue inspections (fire). Additionally with passenger lift inspections, a lift inspection had been missed, resulting in a 16-month delay between inspections.

findings.headline: Significant fraud detected and resolved in 2025-26: £911k notional value, £55k cashable savings
findings.detail: The council's fraud detection and resolution work in 2025-26 identified and resolved cases with a notional value of £911,160 and cashable savings of £54,762. This represents the council's highest fraud savings to date. The council participates in the National Fraud Initiative and has strengthened its approach to fraud management.
findings.matters: Whilst detection is positive, the scale of fraud identified (£911k) signals control or detection weaknesses that may have allowed fraud to persist; ongoing fraud risk is material.
findings.figures: £911,160 notional savings; £54,762 cashable savings from fraud detection and resolution
findings.quote: The Council takes fraud seriously, identifying and resolving cases during 2025/26 with a notional value of £911k and cashable savings of £55k.

findings.headline: £1.45m of savings removed from medium-term financial forecast during budget setting for 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.detail: The council achieved approximately £1.45m of savings through budget challenge sessions and savings initiatives, which were removed from the medium-term financial forecast. However, for 2026-27, the AGS notes that 'recognising the constraints of delivering LGR alongside business-as-usual...a longlist of savings initiatives has been produced, with only those feasible to be delivered in year...being taken forward.' This implies planned savings may not be fully realisable given LGR pressures.
findings.matters: Savings delivery constraints during LGR suggest the council's medium-term budget plan may face headwinds; inability to realise planned savings creates financial resilience risk.
findings.figures: £1.45m savings removed from medium-term financial forecast for 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.quote: Approximately £1.45m of savings have been removed from the medium-tern financial forecast as part of the budget setting process for 2025/26 and 2026/27...Recognising the constraints of delivering LGR alongside its business-as-usual during 2026/27, a longlist of savings initiatives has been produced, with only those feasible to be delivered in year, and which will continue to provide a benefit for the new West Surrey authority, being taken forward for delivery.

findings.headline: New Financial Management System and Housing Management System implemented in 2025-26 with data migration risks and control documentation gaps
findings.detail: The council implemented a new Financial Management System and new Housing Management System modules during 2025-26. Project risks associated with data migration were identified and mitigated by additional audit checks. However, the AGS notes that 'documentation relating to processes and procedures will need to be updated and refined to meet information governance requirements and assure internal controls are in place to prevent errors in data processing and handling.' These actions are listed for follow-up in 2026-27.
findings.matters: System implementation during major organisational change (LGR) carries execution risk; control documentation gaps in financial systems represent a financial reporting and compliance risk.
findings.figures: New Financial Management System; new Housing Management System modules
findings.quote: The organisation has implemented a new Financial Management System and delivered new modules of the integrated Housing Management System during 2025/26. Project risks associated with data migration were identified to be mitigated by additional audit and control checks. It is also recognised that documentation relating to processes and procedures will need to be updated and refined to meet information governance requirements and assure internal controls are in place to prevent errors in data processing and handling.

findings.headline: Active debt restructuring with £19.3m repaid via asset sales at PWLB discounts; further options being explored
findings.detail: The council used receipts from two asset sales to repay borrowing at discounted PWLB rates: £12m in December 2024 (£5.7m discount) and £7.3m in February 2025 (£3.7m discount). The council also set aside additional voluntary repayments. The statement notes the council is 'currently exploring further debt restructuring options' as part of its engagement with MHCLG on debt management.
findings.matters: Active debt management through asset sales and restructuring suggests the council is focused on managing its borrowing position; further restructuring exploration may indicate ongoing debt concerns or opportunity.
findings.figures: £12m repaid December 2024 (£5.7m discount); £7.3m repaid February 2025 (£3.7m discount); combined discounts £9.4m
findings.quote: the Council used the receipts from two asset sales to repay borrowing, making use of significant discounts available via the PWLB. In December 2024 and February 2025, the Council repaid £12m and £7.3m of debt, attracting discounts of £5.7m and £3.7m respectively...The Council is currently exploring further debt restructuring options.

findings.headline: Risk management consistency failures: two service areas did not update risk registers in Q4 2025-26
findings.detail: Despite reminders and reviews, inconsistency in risk management updates was identified in Q4. Specifically, two service areas failed to review or update their service risk register in Q4 2025-26. One senior officer stated in their governance declaration that they were 'not confident that risk monitoring was carried out regularly' or that 'risk controls or mitigation in place could be appropriately evidenced.' This matter is listed for follow-up in 2026-27.
findings.matters: Breakdown in risk monitoring creates control gaps and indicates governance weakness in service-level accountability, particularly during a period of significant organisational change.
findings.figures: Two service areas failed Q4 2025-26 risk register updates
findings.quote: Despite the reminders and reviews, inconsistency in the depth of review and updates provided has been identified in Q4 2025/26 from the review of the risk management system and from statements made in the Annual Governance declaration forms. Two service areas failed to review or update their service risk register in Q4 2025/26.

findings.headline: Council lifted from non-statutory Best Value Notice in December 2024 after quarterly MHCLG engagement
findings.detail: The council operated under a non-statutory Best Value Notice (NS BVN) from MHCLG but the notice was lifted in December 2024. The council has continued quarterly engagement sessions with MHCLG throughout 2025-26, and the NS BVN Programme Board was replaced by a Continuous Improvement Programme Board to monitor ongoing improvement work, including savings and service reviews.
findings.matters: Councils placed under regulatory notice face heightened scrutiny and borrowing risk; ongoing quarterly engagement with MHCLG suggests monitored financial resilience concerns persist.
findings.figures: Non-statutory Best Value Notice lifted December 2024; quarterly MHCLG engagement continuing
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council continued its quarterly engagement sessions with MHCLG following the lifting of its non-statutory Best Value Notice (NS BVN) in December 2024.

findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator issued Consumer grade C4, finding very serious failings
findings.detail: The council made a self-referral to the Regulator of Social Housing in June 2025 after identifying rent-setting issues. Following inspection in February 2026, the regulator issued a Consumer grade C4, the lowest rating. The regulator concluded there are 'very serious failings' in delivering consumer standards outcomes and 'serious failings' in delivering the Rent Standard. The council has set up a formalised improvement programme with corporate resource assigned and the programme now reports to the Continuous Improvement Board.
findings.matters: A regulator's lowest housing grade signals material service and control failures in a significant council function, and remediation efforts may require sustained financial and management investment.
findings.figures: Consumer grade C4; Rent Standard grade: serious failings
findings.quote: The Regulatory Judgement confirms a consumer grade of C4 while also concluding that there are serious failings in how the Council is delivering the outcomes of the Rent Standard.

findings.headline: £368 million of council dwelling and building assets are not annually revalued, creating valuation risk.
findings.detail: Council dwellings (£337m) and other land and buildings (£31m) are not revalued annually. Management did not perform an assessment in the prior year to satisfy itself that carrying amounts were not materially different from current value, contrary to CIPFA Code requirements. This is partially addressed for 2025/26 through indexation implementation.
findings.matters: Large unverified asset values on the balance sheet create uncertainty about the council's true asset base and financial position; revaluation shortfalls could indicate hidden impairments or require future writedowns.
findings.figures: Council dwellings £337m; Other land and buildings £31m
findings.quote: Management did not perform an assessment of assets not revalued (Council dwellings £337m, Other land and building £31m) during the year to satisfy itself that the carrying amounts were not materially different from current value at year-end. This is contrary to the requirements of the CIPFA Code of Practice on Local Authority Accounting.

findings.headline: Multiple material prior-year audit recommendations remain unimplemented or only partially addressed.
findings.detail: Of 12 recommendations from the 2024/25 audit, several remain not addressed or only in progress, including: journal authorization controls (partially addressed only from month 12), internal recharges reporting (not addressed), manual adjustment documentation (£1.176m without evidence, not addressed), and creditor reporting system limitations (not addressed).
findings.matters: Failure to implement audit recommendations indicates either weak management capability or low priority placed on control improvements, both of which concern external lenders assessing governance quality.
findings.figures: 12 recommendations from 2024/25; at least 7 not fully addressed by planning for 2025/26
findings.quote: Due to time and resource constraints faced by management, these matters have not yet been addressed and will therefore be followed up during the year-end fieldwork. Assessment: Not addressed

findings.headline: Adverse regulator finding on social housing delivery identified as a significant VfM weakness.
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued an adverse report in February 2026 on Runnymede's delivery of social housing. The audit plan identifies this as a risk of significant weakness in the council's arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness, requiring additional audit procedures.
findings.matters: A regulator's adverse finding on social housing operations indicates management or operational failings in a significant council function, with potential reputational and financial consequences.
findings.figures: Adverse report issued February 2026
findings.quote: A risk of significant weakness in the Council's arrangements to secure economy, efficiency and effectiveness was identified in response to the adverse findings by the Regulator of Social Housing in the delivery of social housing issued in February 2026.

findings.headline: Disclaimer of opinion issued on prior year accounts means no audit assurance over opening balances for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 audit opinion was a disclaimer due to the backstop date. For 2025/26, this means the auditor will have only limited assurance over opening balances and no assurance over closing reserves, creating uncertainty over the starting position for the current year audit.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on prior year accounts being independently verified, undermining the evidential base for assessing the council's financial position and trends.
findings.figures: Year ended 31 March 2025: disclaimer of opinion issued
findings.quote: In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025, a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the backstop. As a result, we anticipate that for 2025/26: we will have limited assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26... no assurance over the closing reserves balance, due to the uncertainty over their opening amount.

findings.paper_title: Financial Sustainability update report - Final Mar 2026
findings.headline: Internal audit assigned 'reasonable' (not substantial) assurance to financial sustainability controls.
findings.detail: The council's savings and sustainability programme received a 'reasonable assurance' rating from internal audit (May 2025), a mid-tier rating indicating moderate confidence. Although only three low-priority actions were identified (now completed), reasonable assurance rather than substantial assurance suggests audit identified meaningful gaps in either the robustness of controls or the reliability of delivery mechanisms.
findings.matters: A 'reasonable' rather than 'substantial' assurance rating indicates audit concerns about the design or execution of financial controls and savings delivery, suggesting execution and forecasting risks.
findings.figures: Audit rating: reasonable; audit actions: 3 low-priority (completed)
findings.quote: The review received a "reasonable" assurance rating and culminated in just 3 low priority actions being agreed by management, all of which are now completed.

findings.paper_title: Financial Sustainability update report - Final Mar 2026
findings.headline: Service review programme stalled: four of six reviews closed or paused, blocking planned savings.
findings.detail: The council has closed or paused four of six service reviews that were designed to generate savings and efficiencies: Safer Runnymede (deferred pending future opportunities), Community Buildings (explicitly closed due to LGR), Chertsey Museum (descoped from review), and Strategic Facilities/Bold Gemini (still in discovery). The closure rationale repeatedly cites local government reorganisation timescales. This means identified savings initiatives will not be delivered and service improvements are indefinitely deferred.
findings.matters: If planned service reviews do not complete, their anticipated savings will not materialise, worsening the financial position and creating uncertainty about the quality and efficiency of asset/service handover to the successor West Surrey Council.
findings.figures: 4 of 6 service reviews closed or paused; 2 of 6 in discovery phase only
findings.quote: in light of timescales for local government reorganisation, the review has been closed with a view to the future West Surrey Council's strategic decisions around delivery of services.

findings.paper_title: Financial Sustainability update report - Final Mar 2026
findings.headline: £2.1M budget deficit for 2026/27 only partially addressed; gap closure mechanism not explained.
findings.detail: The council identified a £2.1M budget gap to close by end of 2026/27. The 6% challenge exercise identified ~£783K in forecast savings, with ~£217K actually applied to the 2026/27 budget—addressing only ~10% of the stated target. The report claims the MTFS showed a 'much-improved position' but provides no transparency on how or whether the remaining £1.9M gap was closed, leaving ambiguity about the true financial position and reliance on working balances.
findings.matters: A lender needs clear evidence that identified budget shortfalls will be met through credible mechanisms, not obscured by vague claims of improvement without substantiation.
findings.figures: £3.9M opening budget gap; £2.1M to find by end 26/27; £217K applied to 26/27 budget from ~£783K forecast savings
findings.quote: The council started the year with a £3.9M budget gap of which £2.1M needed to be found by the end of 26/27 and a further £1.8M by the end of 2027/28.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs ratio rising from 127% to 156% of revenue stream by 2028-29
findings.detail: The ratio of net financing costs (debt interest net of investment income) to the General Fund revenue stream is projected to rise from 127.83% in 2024-25 to 141.87% in 2026-27 to 156.09% by 2028-29. The paper notes this is high because of 'past borrowing to fund our Investment Strategy and regeneration schemes' but that this income is not counted in the ratio. Even so, the rising trend is concerning.
findings.matters: A ratio above 100% means debt-related costs exceed the main revenue stream; a rising trend suggests the council is becoming increasingly constrained by historic debt decisions, limiting flexibility for new spending or investment.
findings.figures: Ratio of net financing costs to net revenue stream: 2024/25 127.83% → 2026/27 141.87% → 2028/29 156.09%
findings.quote: Ratio of Net Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream: 2024/25 Actual 38.99%, 2025/26 Revised 40.10%, 2026/27 Estimate 46.13%, 2027/28 Estimate 47.84%, 2028/29 Estimate 50.27%. General Fund 127.83%, 112.89%, 141.87%, 146.98%, 156.09%

findings.headline: 38-40% of General Fund income comes from non-financial investments, creating concentration risk
findings.detail: The council's non-financial investment income (primarily regeneration and property schemes) is forecast to be £28,032k out of £74,086k total revenue in 2026-27 (38%). This proportion remains high through the forecast period (down to 30% by 2028-29). A lender needs to understand the sustainability and volatility of this income, especially given that 75% of total external debt relates to non-financial investments.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on commercial/investment income for core budget makes the council vulnerable to property market downturns or asset underperformance; this income is less predictable than council tax or grants.
findings.figures: Non-financial investments income 2026/27 £28,032k out of total revenue £74,086k = 38%. Outstanding non-financial instrument debt £435,963k out of total external debt £587,114k = 74%.
findings.quote: This shows that nearly 40% of all the Council's General Fund income comes from Non -Financial Investment income. Ensuring that these types of investments are managed effectively and addressing the risks associated with them is key.

findings.headline: HRA debt has regular maturities from 2027 onwards with limited repayment plan until 2031
findings.detail: The HRA is financed with PWLB debt described as 'relatively short dated with regular maturities from 2027 (year 2) onwards.' The HRA Business Plan does not begin making voluntary debt repayment until 2031, starting at only £250k/year and rising to £5m/year from 2037. This creates refinancing exposure over the next 6+ years with rising rates.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can refinance HRA debt as it matures, especially if interest rates have not fallen as forecast; delayed repayment means sustained debt service costs.
findings.figures: HRA Business Plan sets aside £250,000 a year from 2031, increasing to £5m from 2037; HRA CFR £100m in 2024/25, projected £90m from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: The HRA has been financed with PWLB debt that is relatively short dated with regular maturities from 2027 (year 2) onwards. The HRA is not required to make MRP. This does not remove the requirement for an authority to consider the debt associated with its HRA and ensure sufficient provision is made over the life of the assets to repay debt. The HRA Business plan starts making provision for repayment of its loans (over and above the statutory limit set-aside) from 2031.

findings.headline: Liquid reserves expected to fall to £2.4m by 2028-29 from £51.3m now, leaving minimal buffer
findings.detail: Expected investment balances are forecast to decline from £51,292k in 2024-25 to £24,011k in 2026-27 to just £2,418k by 2028-29. General Fund reserves fall from £70.8m to £49.3m. HRA reserves collapse from £39.7m to £7.8m. This creates minimal liquidity headroom for unexpected pressures or opportunities.
findings.matters: A lender needs councils to hold adequate reserves against service volatility and to cover debt service if investment income underperforms; reaching £2.4m on a council this size is operationally risky.

findings.headline: Government remains concerned about council debt levels despite not renewing oversight notice
findings.detail: The council received a non-statutory Best Value Notice in December 2023 from MHCLG citing concern over high debt relative to size. In December 2024 (the anniversary), MHCLG confirmed the notice is not being renewed but stated 'the department remains concerned about the significant debt held by the council and the risk this carries' and expects the council to continue steps to reduce debt. This signals ongoing government monitoring rather than clearance.
findings.matters: Active government oversight of debt management indicates regulatory risk and constrains the council's financial flexibility; a lender needs to understand whether the council can meet debt reduction expectations while maintaining service delivery.
findings.figures: NS-BVN received December 2023 after CIPFA review; notice monitoring continued through December 2024
findings.quote: Whilst we are not renewing the notice, the department remains concerned about the significant debt held by the council and the risk this carries... We expect the council to continue taking steps to reduce and manage its overall debt.

findings.headline: Council recently exited Best Value Notice but MHCLG engagement continues
findings.detail: The Council was subject to a non-statutory Best Value Notice (a governance intervention by the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities) between December 2023 and December 2024. Whilst the Notice has been lifted, the paper notes continued engagement with MHCLG in the 12 months following its removal, suggesting ongoing monitoring by central government.
findings.matters: A lender monitors whether councils have been subject to central government intervention; whilst the Notice has been lifted, continued MHCLG engagement indicates the Council remains under scrutiny beyond formal intervention.
findings.figures: Notice period: Dec 2023 to Dec 2024
findings.quote: The Council is no longer subject to a non-statutory Best Value Notice but has continued engagement with MHCLG throughout the 12-month period following lifting of the Notice.

findings.headline: Major structural reorganisation into new unitary authority underway with vesting date 1 April 2027
findings.detail: The Council is preparing to transition into West Surrey unitary authority as part of local government reorganisation (LGR). The paper identifies this as a major change requiring the Council to manage LGR implementation simultaneously with delivering Corporate Business Plan objectives and continuing services. The Council's risk management framework is being applied to accommodate LGR-related risks.
findings.matters: Organisational mergers of this scale pose significant execution risk; service disruption, cost overruns, or governance failures during transition can affect financial stability and borrowing capacity of both the merging and successor authority.
findings.figures: Vesting date: 1 April 2027
findings.quote: ensuring its transition into a new unitary authority for West Surrey from 1st April 2027, must be managed alongside achievement of the aims within the Corporate Business Plan and the continuation of services to its residents. The identification of risk, and the understanding of what level of risk is acceptable, will be essential in achieving these multiple objectives.

findings.headline: Council has formalised a moratorium on debt-funded investment property purchases
findings.detail: The Council has explicitly ended its practice of purchasing investment property (assets bought primarily for yield) using debt funding. The paper links this directly to Financial risk appetite and notes it reflects tightening of the prudential framework following the Levelling Up and Regeneration Act 2023. This removes a source of revenue income that the Council had previously pursued.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether revenue streams from commercial property are being relied upon; the moratorium signals the Council is constraining income sources and may have relied on these yields in prior years.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: the Council formalised its intent not to purchase additional investment property with a moratorium on new debt-funded asset investments, i.e. assets purchased primarily for yield.

findings.headline: Council forecasts a continued budget gap despite improved 2026/27 position
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget report shows improvement in the revenue budget forecast compared to prior years, but the paper explicitly states that a future budget gap continues to be forecast based on current assumptions. The Council acknowledges it must not undermine its successor authority's financial position by taking increased financial risk during the transition period.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs to understand whether deficits are being resolved or merely deferred; a continued forecast gap signals ongoing structural imbalance even if one year improves.
findings.figures: None provided in this paper; reference is made to 'The 2026/27 Budget report'
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Budget report demonstrates an improved position with respect to the forecast revenue budget gap, and potential future working balances however a future budget gap continues to be forecast based on current assumptions. This position will be superseded by the budget for West Surrey Council from 2027/28, but it is incumbent on the Council not to undermine the financial position of its successor authority by taking increased financial risk.

findings.headline: Additional £250,000 committed to LGR implementation with budget flagged as subject to refinement
findings.detail: The council has transferred an additional £250,000 from its Service Transformation Reserve to support local government reorganization implementation (total LGR budget now £487k: £91k 2025/26, £396k 2026/27). The council explicitly notes that LGR costs are subject to change as cost estimates are refined. Identified savings initiatives are being deferred because taking on major new savings initiatives before merger is considered imprudent.
findings.matters: This represents a material drawdown of reserves during a period when reserves are already pressured. More significantly, the council is deferring identified savings because of LGR disruption, meaning identified cost reductions will not be delivered, and LGR costs may exceed budget as plans develop.
findings.figures: Additional £250,000 transfer; total LGR budget £487,000 (£91,000 + £396,000)
findings.quote: Given the likely draw on staff resources to support implementation plans for the new West Surrey Council, and that limited invest-to-save initiatives are anticipated to come forward during the year, it is recommended that an additional £250,000 be directed to provide LGR support.

findings.headline: Staff pay award and grading review create contingent liability against reserves
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes a 3% provision for staff pay awards (covering National Living Wage uplift and cost-of-living increases), contingent on successful union negotiations. A separate pay and grading review is undergoing consultation with unions, with outcomes pending. The council explicitly states that if actual costs exceed budget, the difference will be met by transfers from the General Fund working balance.
findings.matters: Staff costs are material to local authorities. If negotiations result in awards above 3%, or if the pay and grading review adds unforeseen costs, the council must draw on reserves at a time when reserves are already under pressure from other budget gaps.
findings.figures: 3% budget provision for pay award, subject to union negotiations and pay and grading review outcome
findings.quote: Any change to the pay inflation estimates included in this report will be compensated for by an equal movement in the transfers to or from the General Fund working balance, subject to the applicable financial procedure rules.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing strategy creates material interest rate exposure when external refinancing becomes necessary
findings.detail: The council has used internal borrowing (drawing down cash reserves) rather than external borrowing to manage debt costs. Current fixed-rate borrowing averages 2.41%. However, as cash reserves deplete and loans mature, the council must externally refinance at substantially higher rates: 5.78% for 50-year loans and 6.01% for 25-year loans (December 2025). This will significantly increase future debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: The council's financial plan relies on managing down cash reserves through internal borrowing. When external refinancing becomes necessary, interest costs will approximately double, creating material pressure on the revenue budget at a time when the council is already tight on finances.
findings.figures: Current borrowing at 2.41% average; prevailing rates 5.78% (50yr) to 6.01% (25yr)
findings.quote: The downside is that current internal borrowing will likely require conversion to external borrowing as cash balances are consumed, at higher rates than the Council's current borrowing.

findings.headline: £2m estimated deficit on business rates collection for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has estimated a £2m deficit on business rates income, representing the variance between estimated and actual collections in the prior year. While this will be compensated from the Business Rates Reserve, it reflects actual collection shortfall and indicates business rates yield in the district is performing below forecast.
findings.matters: Business rates are a core income source. A £2m collection shortfall indicates lower-than-expected business activity in the district and is a leading indicator of local economic conditions. Recurring shortfalls erode the financial position.
findings.figures: initial estimate of a £2m deficit
findings.quote: At the time of writing this report, this work is in progress and an initial estimate of a £2m deficit has been included in the budget. Any material changes to the estimates within the budget will be compensated for from the Business Rates Reserve.

findings.headline: Core Spending Power cut by 14.3% in 2025/26, the third-largest reduction nationally among 349 English councils
findings.detail: The change in funding methodology has resulted in Runnymede's Core Spending Power falling from £16.1m in 2024/25 to £13.8m in 2025/26 (14.3% reduction). A partial recovery to £14.0m in 2026/27 is still 12.5% below 2024/25 levels. Runnymede has been identified as the third-most impacted authority nationally.
findings.matters: This represents a fundamental reduction in resources available to the council to fund services. The council is responding with significant savings programmes and reliance on reserves to bridge the gap, indicating structural financial stress.
findings.figures: CSP fell from £16.1m to £13.8m (14.3% reduction), recovery to £14.0m for 2026/27 (12.5% below 2024/25)
findings.quote: This is the third largest reduction in funding across the period 2024/25 to 2028/29 of any of the 349 English authorities with comparable data.

findings.headline: Wholly-owned property company (RBCI) unable to make interest payments, putting £2.1m annual budgeted income at risk
findings.detail: RBCI, the council's wholly-owned residential property management company, was unable to make its last interest payment due to cash flow issues. The council is exploring a revised funding model that would reduce the company's loan liability, but this is explicitly noted as likely to reduce the interest income received by the council.
findings.matters: The revenue budget assumes £2.1m per annum interest income from RBCI loans. If this income is reduced or delayed, it creates a significant budget gap that must be filled by additional savings or reserve draw-down at a time when reserves are already under pressure.
findings.figures: over £2.1m per annum in interest from loans to RBCI
findings.quote: RBCI was unable to make its last interest payment due to cash flow issues. The Council has approved exploration of a revised funding model for RBCI, which would seek to reduce the loan liability of the company, support its cash flow requirements and improve its financial sustainability.

findings.headline: The council acknowledges that property tenancies are becoming harder to secure, creating income risk on its investment portfolio.
findings.detail: The council states that 'strong long-term tenancies are increasingly difficult to find, so reductions can often become apparent in the short to medium term'. To mitigate this, it holds 'an income equalisation reserve and a property maintenance reserve' to 'even out future year's income and expenditure'.
findings.matters: Difficulty in securing reliable tenants increases the risk that investment property income will fall, affecting the general fund revenue budget; this is a constraint on financial stability.
findings.figures: No specific income volatility figures disclosed; reserves exist but levels not stated
findings.quote: strong long-term tenancies are increasingly difficult to find, so reductions can often become apparent in the short to medium term

findings.headline: The council has banned borrowing to buy investment property, moving away from income-generation investments.
findings.detail: The council has 'formalised its intent not to purchase additional investment property by placing a moratorium on new debt-funded asset investments'. It acknowledges that 'Borrowing for purely income generation reasons has now ceased and the investment property portfolio has moved into the asset management phase'.
findings.matters: The council previously used property acquisitions to replace income lost during regeneration projects; this option is now closed, limiting its ability to mitigate revenue impacts of major developments.
findings.figures: No details of current investment property portfolio size or rental income
findings.quote: the Council has formalised its intent not to purchase additional investment property by placing a moratorium on new debt-funded asset investments i.e. assets purchased primarily for yield.

findings.headline: The council received a Non-Statutory Best Value Notice from MHCLG in December 2023.
findings.detail: The document discloses that the council 'receipt of a Non-Statutory Best Value Notice in December 2023 and on-going engagement with MHCLG subsequent to the notice not being renewed in December 2024'. A Best Value Notice is issued when government has concerns about a council's financial management or service delivery.
findings.matters: A Best Value Notice signals that MHCLG had concerns about the council's performance or financial position; this affects creditworthiness assessment even though the notice was not renewed.
findings.figures: No specific findings or remedial actions disclosed
findings.quote: following receipt of a Non-Statutory Best Value Notice in December 2023 and on-going engagement with MHCLG subsequent to the notice not being renewed in December 2024

findings.headline: The council's capital programme is heavily dependent on selling assets because borrowing is now constrained.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states: 'The future of the Capital Programme is heavily dependent on the production of new capital receipts; which is increasingly important where future borrowing may be restricted'. This dependency creates execution risk if the council cannot sell assets at anticipated prices or timing.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial resilience needs to understand that capital spending now depends on a variable revenue stream (asset sales) rather than planned borrowing, introducing execution risk.
findings.figures: No specific capital receipt targets or capital programme size disclosed
findings.quote: The future of the Capital Programme is heavily dependent on the production of new capital receipts; which is increasingly important where future borrowing may be restricted

findings.headline: MHCLG has told the council to reduce its existing borrowing levels, making it difficult to access new borrowing for capital projects.
findings.detail: The council states that 'MHCLG has indicated it would like to see our existing borrowing levels reduced so accessing funds in this way may be difficult'. This appears in multiple sections as a constraint on the council's capital programme. The council is 'already committed to exploring measures to reduce its overall level of debt'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot rely on traditional borrowing to fund capital projects; this forces reliance on asset sales or external funding and indicates government concerns about the council's debt levels.
findings.figures: No current borrowing figures disclosed in this document
findings.quote: MHCLG has indicated it would like to see our existing borrowing levels reduced so accessing funds in this way may be difficult.

findings.headline: Portfolio has accumulated £166.6m in capital value losses since purchase despite recent stabilisation
findings.detail: The portfolio shows cumulative capital depreciation of £166.6m from purchase cost to current valuation (improved from £173.1m loss prior year). While recent 12-month capital growth of 4.44% shows stabilisation, the accumulated loss constrains the council's optionality for strategic asset disposals and indicates long-term value destruction from the original investment programme (2015-2020).
findings.matters: Large unrealised losses constrain ability to realise the asset disposal programme now necessary for debt reduction; accumulated loss increases LTV risk and limits refinancing options
findings.figures: Capital loss -£166.6m cumulative since purchase; capital growth 4.44% (last 12 months); current portfolio valuation £348.9m vs original £515.5m+
findings.quote: KPI 007 Capital Appreciation/Reduction Difference in Capital Values, since purchase £-166,583,823 (Previous year £-173,148,554)

findings.headline: Quarterly vacancy income loss of £444k with multiple assets remaining vacant
findings.detail: Q2 generated £444,108 income loss through vacancies, with specific properties remaining vacant including Osprey House, Pine Trees ground/first floor, units in Addlestone One and Magna Square, Charter Place, The Precinct, and multiple Station Road units. Vacancy rate of 5.7% is below benchmark but represents deferred income recovery.
findings.matters: Sustained multi-asset vacancies indicate tenant demand weakness; unreleased space defers revenue recovery and could signal capital value impairment
findings.figures: £444,108 quarterly income loss from vacancy; vacancy rate 5.7% (improved from 6.12% Q1); market rental value of vacancies £444k+
findings.quote: Therefore, the total loss of income in the investment portfolio through vacancy quarter 2 is £444,108...Some notable vacancies include: • Osprey House • Grnd & 1st floor Building 5 Pine Trees • Units in Addlestone One and Magna Square • Charter Place • The Precinct

findings.headline: General Fund revenue heavily dependent on property investment returns, which represent nearly 34% of all income
findings.detail: The investment portfolio contributed £29.252m to the General Fund against total General Fund income of £75.987m in 2024/25. The council notes this dependency means it is critical that investment assets are managed effectively to ensure long-term financial sustainability.
findings.matters: High revenue dependency on commercial property performance exposes the council to portfolio volatility; any sustained income reduction would create a significant budget shortfall
findings.figures: Investment income £29.252m (net of VAT); total General Fund income £75.987m; nearly 34% of General Fund revenue from investments
findings.quote: This shows that nearly 34% of all the Council's General Fund income last year came from property investment income. Ensuring that these types of investments are managed effectively and addressing the risks associated with them is key to the future sustainability of the authority.

findings.headline: Over half the portfolio is concentrated in office sector facing ongoing structural market challenges
findings.detail: Office assets comprise 51.66% of the portfolio by capital value, making the portfolio unbalanced and highly susceptible to office market performance. While the council's South East office holdings are outperforming the market benchmark, the sector continues to reflect structural headwinds from hybrid working and over-supply.
findings.matters: Concentration risk amplifies exposure to sector-wide downturns; office sector faces structural secular decline that could erode revenue and asset values
findings.figures: Office 51.66% of portfolio capital value; South East office holdings achieved 9.1% total return vs -1.8% benchmark; office capital growth only -1.0%
findings.quote: the portfolio is heavily weighted to offices by both number of properties and capital value, this shows the portfolio is not a traditionally balanced portfolio so is much more susceptible to changes within the office sector than a balanced portfolio might be.

findings.headline: Portfolio has short average lease term of 7.0 years with major tenant expirations concentrated in 2027-2028
findings.detail: MSCI benchmarking shows the average unexpired lease term is 7.0 years compared with the market benchmark of 13.8 years, reflecting that long-standing leases are approaching expiry. The council explicitly notes upcoming lease events in 2027–2028 that require active management. The income erosion schedule shows 27.7% of rental income at risk in 2028.
findings.matters: Lease expirations concentrate refinancing and tenant replacement risk; failure to relet at current market rates would reduce revenue and asset valuations
findings.figures: Average unexpired lease term 7.0 years (benchmark 13.8 years); lease erosion to Mar 2028 of 27.7% of rental income; lease erosion to Mar 2029 of 6.9%
findings.quote: The MSCI data shows that the average unexpired lease term across the portfolio is 7.0 years, compared with 13.8 years for the benchmark. This reflects that several long-standing leases are approaching expiry...Work is ongoing to actively manage upcoming lease events and maintain occupancy levels, particularly ahead of expiries in 2027–2028.

findings.headline: Loan-to-value ratio of 133% means investment property debt exceeds asset value
findings.detail: The portfolio has a loan-to-value ratio of 133% (down marginally from 134% prior year), indicating the council's outstanding borrowings exceed the current valuation of the investment assets. This represents a high-risk position that constrains financial flexibility.
findings.matters: LTV over 100% creates covenant risk and limits the council's ability to refinance or raise additional borrowing; it also leaves the council exposed if asset values fall further
findings.figures: LTV 133% (previous year 134%); total investment property valuation £348.9m as at March 2025
findings.quote: KPI 008 Loan to Value ratio Amount of debt compared to the total asset value. 133%

findings.headline: Council planning material asset disposals to reduce borrowing as part of local government reorganisation
findings.detail: Following confirmation that Runnymede will merge into the West Surrey authority, the council identifies reduction of borrowing and associated liabilities as a key strategic priority. The Assets & Regeneration team is explicitly considering the disposal of commercial assets to alleviate borrowing costs and improve financial resilience against a backdrop of economic uncertainty.
findings.matters: Material disposals would significantly reduce revenue generation and debt service capacity, with knock-on effects for the council's revenue budget sustainability
findings.figures: 30 investment properties held; 2 currently under offer for sale; property investment income £29.252m annually (nearly 34% of General Fund)
findings.quote: A key strategic focus for the property team moving forward will be the reduction of borrowing and the long-term liabilities associated with managing a large commercial portfolio. This may necessitate the disposal of certain commercial assets to alleviate borrowing costs and improve financial resilience.

findings.headline: Chertsey Museum stores project hit structural constraints requiring redesign and additional work, illustrating capital scheme delivery risk.
findings.detail: The approved lease of The Orchard to store the museum collection hit an obstacle: an external structural engineer's report showed roller-racking cannot be installed in planned spaces without expensive reinforcement. Officers are now considering alternative approaches, including different spaces for roller-racking and static shelving, plus seeking grant funding. An update to members will be provided once resolved, with potential approval sought for any changes.
findings.matters: Capital schemes hitting unforeseen delivery obstacles can escalate costs and create timeline slippage, tying up management resources during a period of budget pressure.
findings.figures: No cost impact stated yet
findings.quote: officers are considering different approaches to resolving this after the commissioned external load bearing report presented some challenges to the desired approach. The report made clear that roller-racking was unable to be installed in the planned spaces without extensive structural work to reinforce the floors.

findings.headline: £2.1m 6% Challenge savings exercise completed in submissions but still in 'steer only' phase with no decisions taken.
findings.detail: All Corporate Heads submitted proposals to identify 6% of controllable budgets (£2.1m). Submissions have been reviewed by Corporate Leadership Team and are now under review by Council Leadership. Feedback will then be given back to heads of service, with a more comprehensive savings list promised by the next committee update. At this stage, no decisions have been made and any changes will follow governance processes.
findings.matters: The savings plan remains aspirational pending political decision; delays in finalizing savings could jeopardise the deadline for bridging the 2026/27 deficit.
findings.figures: £2.1m to be saved (6% of controllable spend)
findings.quote: At the time of this report all 6% submissions have been made. They have been initially reviewed by the Corporate Leadership Team and are now under review with Council Leadership. Feedback and steer will then be given to the heads of service on their submissions. It is forecast that by the next update to O&S committee, a more comprehensive list of savings, efficiency and income details will be available. It should be noted that at this stage any submissions are purely for steer only, no decisions have been taken.

findings.headline: Service Transformation Reserve has been depleted to £420k from £1m opening balance, limiting future invest-to-save capacity.
findings.detail: The £1m reserve created in 2024 to pump-prime transformation savings has committed £580k to various initiatives including devolution support (£250k), Best Value Notice response (£125k), pay review (£30k), and other projects. Projected closing balance at 31 March 2026 is £420k. The report notes that as more complex schemes come forward, draw-down is likely to increase.
findings.matters: Rapid depletion of the transformation reserve reduces the council's ability to fund future efficiency gains and signals reliance on one-time resources to bridge structural budget gaps.
findings.figures: Opening balance £1m; projected closing balance £420k (£580k committed); individual drawdowns: Devolution £250k, NS BVN £125k, Financial Inclusion £70k, Pay and Grading £30k, Company refinancing £40k, Parking restructure £30k, Parking vehicle £25k, Copilot pilot £10k
findings.quote: Opening balance as at 1st April 2024: 1,000,000 ... Projected closing balance at 31st March 2026: 420,000

findings.headline: Council faces a £3.9m three-year budget gap with £2.1m due by end of 2026/27, now worsened by supplementary estimates.
findings.detail: The council started the year with a £3.9m deficit across the medium term (£2.1m by 2026/27, then £1.8m in 2027/28). However, additional cost pressures and supplementary estimates approved during the year have made the position worse, though the exact revised gap will be shown in an updated MTFS in November. No revised figure is stated in this update.
findings.matters: An expanding budget gap that has not been fully closed by current savings initiatives signals financial stress and limits the council's flexibility.
findings.figures: £3.9m total gap; £2.1m due by end of 2026/27; £1.8m due in 2027/28; revised position TBC
findings.quote: The Council started the year with a £3.9m budget gap of which £2.1m needed to be found by the end of 26/27 and a further £1.8m by the end of 2027/28. Whilst significant progress has now been made against the original target, additional commitments and cost pressures including the approval of several large supplementary estimates have offset them.

findings.headline: RBC Investments Ltd (a council wholly-owned company) defaulted on a scheduled interest payment and resolution has stalled.
findings.detail: The council's subsidiary failed to pay £309,000 of interest due on 3 July 2025. The payment remains outstanding. Officers anticipated quicker resolution of 'capital structure issues' but progress has been slower than expected and the council is only at stage two of agreed remedial actions, requiring further legal and due diligence advice. The council has outstanding loans to RBC entities totalling approximately £38m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council faces a material problem in recovering income from a subsidiary it is financing. A £309k missed payment and delayed resolution suggests the underlying property investments may be underperforming or in financial difficulty.
findings.figures: Outstanding interest payment of £309,000; total loans to RBC Investments entities: Development Loans £38.2mln (split across Addlestone One £25.3mln, Magna Square £11.8mln, Other £1mln), Working Capital Loans £3.7mln
findings.quote: RBC Investments Ltd did not make the scheduled interest payment of £309,000 on 03 July 2025 and this balance remains outstanding. Progress on resolving the capital structure issues at RBC Investments Ltd has been slower than anticipated and officers are currently in the process of stage two of the agreed actions in seeking further legal and due diligence advice.

findings.headline: Government continues to express concern about the council's debt levels relative to its size, despite not renewing the formal Best Value Notice.
findings.detail: In December 2023, the council received a non-statutory Best Value Notice flagging concern about high debt relative to its size. A year later, in December 2024, MHCLG confirmed they remain concerned about 'the significant debt held by the council and the risk this carries' and expect the council to continue reducing and managing its debt. The council responded by removing future borrowing from its capital programme and paying down debt where prudent.
findings.matters: Government-expressed concern about debt is a warning signal to lenders that the council is operating under scrutiny and may face regulatory intervention if debt management does not improve.
findings.figures: Council's CFR at year-end estimate £679mln; total borrowings as at 30 September 2025 were £587.4mln, down from £597.7mln opening balance
findings.quote: In December 2024, on the anniversary of the receipt of the NS-BVN, MHCLG stated that 'Whilst we are not renewing the notice, the department remains concerned about the significant debt held by the council and the risk this carries', and that 'We expect the council to continue taking steps to reduce and manage its overall debt.'

findings.headline: External audits for 2019/20 to 2022/23 remain incomplete despite the 2024/25 accounts being published on time
findings.detail: The council resolved a prior-year weakness by publishing its 2024/25 unaudited financial statements by the 30 June 2025 deadline. However, the auditor notes that "At the time of writing the external audits for 2019/20 to 2022/23 remain incomplete as the previous external auditor has yet to complete their audit and issue their opinions." This creates an extended period of unaudited or unfinalized historical accounts.
findings.matters: A lender relies on audited accounts for assurance over historical financial position. Incomplete external audits for multiple prior years create uncertainty about the reliability of the historical record and may suggest prior issues with accounts preparation.
findings.figures: Audits for 2019/20, 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 incomplete; 2024/25 accounts published 30 June 2025
findings.quote: At the time of writing the external audits for 2019/20 to 2022/23 remain incomplete as the previous external auditor has yet to complete their audit and issue their opinions.

findings.headline: The council reduced borrowing by £41 million in 2024/25 through debt repayment, but this includes one-off refinancing gains of £9.4 million that will not recur
findings.detail: Total borrowings fell from £628 million to £598 million. The council increased Minimum Revenue Provision and Voluntary Revenue Provision by approximately £2 million per annum. Additionally, the council secured a £5.7 million discount on early repayment of £12 million in debt and a £3.7 million discount on repayment of £7.3 million in debt, taking advantage of favourable interest rate conditions. These discounts are non-recurring gains.
findings.matters: While debt reduction is positive, a lender must distinguish between sustainable debt service improvements and one-off gains from refinancing. The underlying rate of debt reduction matters more than the headline figure.
findings.figures: £41 million borrowing reduction; £5.7 million one-off refinancing discount; £3.7 million one-off refinancing discount; annual MRP/VRP increase approximately £2 million
findings.quote: The favourable gap between current borrowing rates and those of existing loans enabled the Council to secure a £5.7 million discount on the early repayment of £12 million in debt and a £3.7million discount on the repayment of a £7.3 million debt.

findings.headline: General fund balances of over £21 million (four times minimum requirement) provide strong financial resilience but hide continued dependence on commercial property income for service delivery
findings.detail: The council ended 2024/25 with general fund balances of over £21 million, which is four times its minimum target, and the Housing Revenue Account also holds £39.6 million. However, £26 million of the £4.7 million 2024/25 surplus came from commercial property income, demonstrating that day-to-day service delivery depends on the performance of a property investment portfolio now subject to a moratorium on new borrowing-funded additions.
findings.matters: Reserves are healthy in absolute terms but the underlying business model remains exposed to property market, interest rate, and occupancy risks. A lender needs to understand whether reserves can absorb a downturn in commercial property income.
findings.figures: General fund balance £21 million (four times minimum); HRA working balances £39.6 million; property portfolio rental income £26 million; 2024/25 surplus £4.7 million
findings.quote: The properties generated £26 million in rental income, in 2024/25, which was used to deliver both statutory and discretionary services.

findings.headline: Council faces a £3.9 million medium-term funding gap requiring £2.1 million in savings by end of 2025/26, with the auditor warning that future savings will be harder to achieve
findings.detail: Despite achieving a £4.7 million surplus in 2024/25 (against a £650k original estimate), the Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a revenue budget gap of £3.9 million by end 2027/28. The council has delivered £3.7 million of savings over two years but must now deliver £2.1 million by end 2025/26 and a further £1.8 million in 2026/27. The auditor explicitly states that future savings "will be harder to realise, requiring more complex initiatives."
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council can close projected deficits without drawing down reserves unsustainably. Acknowledging that future savings are harder to find raises questions about delivery risk.
findings.figures: £3.9 million gap by 2027/28; £2.1 million savings required by end 2025/26; £1.8 million in 2026/27; £3.7 million delivered over past two years
findings.quote: future savings will be harder to realise, requiring more complex initiatives

findings.headline: Central government remains concerned about the council's £598 million debt burden backed by a £350.8 million property portfolio
findings.detail: The council received a Non-Statutory Best Value Notice in December 2023 over high debt levels and £20 million annual reliance on commercial income. Although the notice was lifted in December 2024, MHCLG stated they "remain concerned about the significant debt held by the Council and the risk this carries" and expect the council to continue its own improvement journey in reducing and managing debt. The council established a moratorium on new debt-funded asset investments in response.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the debt burden is manageable and whether continued dependence on commercial income creates unacceptable sector risk.
findings.figures: £598 million long-term debt (down from £628 million in 2023/24); £350.8 million investment property portfolio; £26 million annual rental income in 2024/25
findings.quote: MHCLG stated that they "remain concerned about the significant debt held by the Council and the risk this carries. As a result, we [MHCLG] expect the Council to continue leading its own improvement journey and taking steps to reduce and manage its overall debt."

findings.headline: Treasury management income £700,000 below budget due to lower interest rates and reduced internal balances
findings.detail: The council's treasury income is running £700k behind budget. This is driven by lower anticipated interest rates and lower cash balances than forecast, reflecting increased use of internal borrowing (using cash reserves) rather than taking out new external loans when existing borrowings mature.
findings.matters: Lower treasury income reduces the council's unallocated resources and may increase future borrowing needs.
findings.figures: £700,000 forecast shortfall in treasury income
findings.quote: Income from treasury management activities is estimated to be £700,000 lower than originally anticipated, This is due to a combination of a drop in anticipated average interest rates and lower balances than originally anticipated due to the increased use of internal borrowing

findings.headline: Insurance commission liability of up to £185,000 arising from high court ruling on cinemas
findings.detail: Following a high court ruling in the London Trocadero LLP v Picturehouse Cinemas LTD case, the council faces a potential liability for insurance commission repayments of up to £185,000. Officers are currently investigating to assess the council's exposure, meaning the final liability remains uncertain.
findings.matters: This represents a material unquantified financial exposure that could require reserve drawdown depending on the investigation outcome.
findings.figures: Potential liability up to £185,000
findings.quote: potential insurance commission repayments of up to £185,000 following recent high court ruling (London Trocadero LLP v Picturehouse Cinemas LTD (2025)). Officers are currently investigating this issue to assess our liability.

findings.headline: General Fund balance reported as £21.1m but unaudited; accounts last signed off by auditors for 2018/19
findings.detail: The council's stated General Fund reserve of £21.1m at April 2025 is unaudited. The most recent audited accounts are for 2018/19, meaning the reserve position has not been independently verified for six years. This creates uncertainty about the actual starting position for the medium-term financial strategy.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on the stated reserve balance as a floor for financial stability if it has not been audited in six years. Any audit adjustments would affect the council's actual financial position.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £21.1m (unaudited); last audited accounts 2018/19
findings.quote: Members will be aware that the last set of the Council's Statement of Accounts to have been signed off by the external auditors are for 2018/19, meaning that the Council's reserve balances as reported in the budget and MTFS could be subject to change should the auditors find any issues.

findings.headline: Investment property rental income – the largest revenue source – faces collection risk and energy compliance uncertainties
findings.detail: The council budgets £25.1m in net rental income from its investment property portfolio, described as 'by far the biggest income generator'. The council is reducing its bad debt provision from 5% to 3% based on recent experience, creating a £567k income gain. However, the paper itself warns of two risks: the ability to relet properties at current rental levels and sustainability issues to ensure the portfolio meets energy regulations.
findings.matters: This single revenue stream represents nearly a quarter of the council's budget. The paper's own caveats about rental relets and energy compliance suggest the income projection may be optimistic.
findings.figures: £25.1m budgeted rental income; bad debt provision reduced from 5% to 3%; £567k betterment from reduction
findings.quote: Although this report sets out an increase in income over the budgeted figures there is still a need to be wary in regard to: • the ability to relet properties at current rental levels • sustainability issues ensuring that the portfolio is compliant with energy regulations

findings.headline: Capital programme financing heavily dependent on asset sales with explicit warning of scheme delays if sales do not materialise
findings.detail: The council's capital programme relies on generating capital receipts from sales of development properties and assets. The budget assumes £4.1m in receipts for the year, but only £2.2m had been generated by September. Looking ahead, non-set-aside capital receipts are projected to drop to just under £3m by 2027/28, with no buffer if market conditions change.
findings.matters: Capital delivery depends on property sales activity over which the council has limited control. Failure to achieve assumed sales would require scheme delays or alternative funding methods.
findings.figures: Capital receipts assumed £4.1m; achieved to Sept £2.2m; non-set-aside receipts projected to drop to 'just under £3m by 2027/28'
findings.quote: Should sales activity not be forthcoming over the period, it will be necessary to delay some capital schemes or find alternative methods of funding for them.

findings.headline: Supplementary estimates creating ongoing spending commitments while council needs £3.9m in savings by March 2028
findings.detail: The council has approved £875k in supplementary estimates in-year with ongoing effects of £608k in 2026/27 and £438k in 2027/28. These include restructures, pay awards, legal resource reviews, and governance activities. The paper explicitly flags this as a concern given the council started the year needing £3.9m in savings to close a budget gap by March 2028, yet new savings identified are limited (£325.5k net for current year, £221.1k from 2026/27 onwards).
findings.matters: Recurring commitments are constraining the council's ability to close a structural budget gap, putting medium-term reserves under pressure.
findings.figures: Supplementary estimates £875k (current year), £608k (2026/27), £438k (2027/28); savings needed to March 2028: £3.9m; new savings identified: £325.5k (current year), £221.1k (from 2026/27)
findings.quote: of most concern is the level of supplementary estimates that have been approved during the year which carry ongoing commitments not just for Runnymede, but for the successor authority under Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Pessimistic scenario (Scenario 3) shows balances falling to £6.4m by end of 2028/29 and eroded by end of 2029/30
findings.detail: The document presents three forecast scenarios. Scenario 3 (pessimistic) models a 2% reduction in commercial income, higher LGR costs, and the upper-end estimates for pay and grading review costs (£1m per annum from July 2026). Under this scenario, the budget deficit reaches £7.2m by 2028/29 and general fund balances are completely eroded by end of 2029/30.
findings.matters: The downside scenario illustrates how quickly the council's position could deteriorate under realistic stress conditions (income decline, cost overruns), with no buffer remaining by 2029/30.
findings.figures: Scenario 3 deficit by 2028/29: £7.2m; Revenue balances by 2028/29: £6.4m (only £1.4m above minimum); balances eroded completely by end 2029/30
findings.quote: Under this scenario, the budget deficit is increased to £7.2m by the close of 2028/29 with revenue balances standing at £6.4m, some £1.4m above the recommended minimum threshold. Without corrective action, balances would fall away completely by the close of 2029/30.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation implementation costs of £419,000 with final allocation across councils not yet determined
findings.detail: Runnymede will cease to exist as a local authority on 1 April 2027 and merge into a West Surrey unitary authority. Implementation costs are estimated at £419,000 (£90k in 2025/26, £329k in 2026/27) including leadership costs, IT consolidation, elections to the shadow authority, and implementation team costs. However, the methodology for distributing these costs across predecessor councils has not yet been agreed, creating uncertainty.
findings.matters: The final council will inherit any budget deficits and unresolved issues; LGR costs and the uncertainty around final allocation adds to the financial pressure on the successor authority.
findings.figures: Estimated LGR implementation costs: £419,000 total (£90,000 in 2025/26; £329,000 in 2026/27); final allocation to be determined
