findings.quote: An estimate of implementation costs was included in the successful 2-unitary bid submission and these costs are anticipated to be shared across all of the existing councils, in a proportion yet to be determined. A provision of £419,000 has therefore been included in the forecast as part of the growth items as while the amount may differ, there is certainty that costs will be incurred.

findings.headline: Council Tax capped at 2.99% increase annually with harmonisation to unitary baseline likely to impose larger increases from April 2027
findings.detail: The council can only increase its share of council tax by 2.99% to avoid a referendum requirement, limiting revenue raising. More significantly, Runnymede currently has the lowest council tax of all Districts and Boroughs in Surrey; under the Council Tax harmonisation exercise for the new unitary authority from April 2027, local residents will face 'a larger percentage increase' to align with other areas.
findings.matters: While current increases are modest, residents face a likely sharp increase post-April 2027, which may create political friction for the successor authority and limit the council's control over this revenue stream.
findings.figures: Current increase: 2.99% (just below 3% referendum trigger); Band D amount: £196.14 (proposed increase of £5.86 to £202.00); additional income 2026/27: £210,037
findings.quote: As Runnymede's Council Tax is currently the lowest of all Districts and Boroughs in Surrey, it is likely that local residents will face a larger percentage increase under this process

findings.headline: Business rates funding reset in 2026/27 with baseline reduction and no pooling gain, combined with New Homes Bonus scrapping
findings.detail: Government funding assumptions include a reduction in business rates income following the anticipated reset of funding baselines, no gain from business rates pooling following the reset (due to tightening of prudential framework), and scrapping of the New Homes Bonus Scheme. Transition arrangements are expected but provide only modest funding floor protection, with larger decreases anticipated in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Government funding reductions from multiple sources in 2026/27-2027/28 create a structural funding pressure that interacts with the underlying budget deficit.
findings.figures: Business rates baseline reset in 2026/27; New Homes Bonus scrapped; funding floor expected to limit drops but with larger decrease anticipated in 2027/28
findings.quote: The forecast therefore assumes a reduction in business rates income in 2026/27, following the anticipated reset of funding baselines within the system, no gain from Business Rates Pooling following the reset, the scrapping of the New Homes Bonus Scheme and a funding floor that sees only a marginal drop in overall anticipated funding in 2026/27 but with a larger decrease in 2027/28

findings.headline: Pay and grading review creates unquantified cost pressure of £500,000 to £1,000,000 per annum if implemented
findings.detail: The council has approved a formal job evaluation scheme and new pay structure pending trade union consultation. While the financial impact is not yet included in the forecast (as it has not been approved), estimates suggest implementation costs of £500k-£1m annually in year one, thereafter subject to inflationary pressures. This is flagged as a significant financial risk to the reserve position.
findings.matters: An unresolved cost pressure of this magnitude could materially worsen the budget position and is being held as a contingency risk, suggesting financial headroom is tighter than headline figures suggest.
findings.figures: Estimated cost of pay and grading review implementation: £500,000-£1,000,000 per annum recurring in year 1
findings.quote: it is estimated to be in the region of £500,000 - £1,000,000 per annum recurring to base cost in year 1 of implementation, thereafter subject to annual inflationary pressures

findings.headline: Outstanding debt of £487.4m on General Fund with past Best Value Notice due to debt levels and commercial income reliance
findings.detail: The council received a non-statutory Best Value Notice (NS-BVN) in December 2023 due to concerns about debt relative to size and reliance on commercial income. The Notice was not renewed at 12-month review, but there is explicit risk that further notices or statutory intervention could be issued if the council does not continue debt reduction. Debt remains at £487.4m (General Fund) as of September 2025.
findings.matters: Government has previously flagged debt concerns; ongoing monitoring and potential re-intervention risk suggests lenders should understand regulatory pressure and the council's vulnerability to external scrutiny.
findings.figures: Total debt at 31 Sept 2025: £587.4m (£487.4m General Fund, £100m HRA); Average General Fund borrowing rate: 2.41%; MRP requirement rising from £5.3m in 2025/26 to £6m medium-term
findings.quote: In December 2023, the Council received a non-statutory Best value Notice (NS-BVN) from government, outlining concerns around debt relative to size, and reliance on commercial income as a substantial revenue source... there is a risk that a further Notice could be issued, or statutory intervention taken, should the Council not continue to deliver continuous improvement, including debt reduction

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio of £350.8m generating declining net income from known lease breaks and asset disposals
findings.detail: The investment property portfolio is a major revenue source (£9.3m net income currently) but is in 'managed decline'. From 2028/29 onwards the council anticipates significant lease breaks for key income-generating assets and potential asset sales. Feasibility work is underway on several properties but no confirmed options are included in the forecast yet.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about reliance on a declining income stream without confirmed replacement revenue, particularly as the asset base shrinks through sales.
findings.figures: Portfolio value: £350.8m; Gross income 2025/26: £28.9m; Net income 2025/26: £9.3m; Projected net income 2026/27: £8.6m; 2027/28: £7.1m; 2028/29 onwards: significant further reductions anticipated
findings.quote: commercial income (before borrowing costs are applied) is projected to see a reduction from 2028/29 due to anticipated void or holding costs, significant lease breaks for key income generating assets and the potential sale of some commercial assets

findings.headline: General Fund working balance forecast to fall below £5m minimum threshold by end of 2029/30
findings.detail: The council's unearmarked reserves, currently at £23.187m, are projected to decline to £21.895m in 2026/27, £18.272m in 2027/28, and fall below the £5m prudent minimum by 2029/30. By 2030/31 balances are forecast to be negative at (£3.906m) without corrective action.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits the council's ability to absorb further shocks and indicates reliance on one-off fixes rather than structural solutions.
findings.quote: Without corrective action the balance will fall marginally below the recommended minimum threshold of £5m towards the end of 2029/30 and be completely eroded during 2030/31.

findings.headline: Budget deficit of £1.29m in 2026/27, growing to £8.1m by 2030/31 without corrective action
findings.detail: The council's revenue budget shows an improving position for 2026/27 (down from £2.1m deficit) but begins deteriorating significantly thereafter. By 2028/29 the deficit is forecast at over £5.6m (from base scenario), and continues worsening to £8.1m by 2030/31. This reflects inflation outpacing income growth annually.
findings.matters: A lender would see an organisation facing structural budget gaps that require continuous drawdown of reserves, reducing financial resilience and raising sustainability questions.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £1.29m deficit; 2027/28: £3.6m deficit; 2028/29 onwards: increasing deficits; by 2030/31: £8.1m deficit without corrective action
findings.quote: the remaining years of the forecast see an on-going draw on the General Fund Working Balance with the budget deficit growing to £8.1m by 2030/31 without further corrective action

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: Staffing recruitment and retention difficulties in key roles over past five years
findings.detail: The council reports five years of difficulty recruiting and retaining experienced staff in housing roles. This presents operational risk for rent collection, tenant services, and financial management of the £100m asset base.
findings.matters: Staffing gaps directly affect rent collection efficiency, compliance with regulatory standards, and asset management quality. Key-role vacancies can lead to service failures and reputational damage.
findings.figures: 5-year recruitment and retention challenges in key roles
findings.quote: As an organisation on the edge of London, RBC has experienced difficulties over the past 5 years in recruiting and retaining experienced staff to key roles.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: Aging flat stock from the 1960s (27% of portfolio) requires intensive capital investment and safety work over next five years
findings.detail: Flats represent 23% of council stock (648 units), with a significant proportion built in the 1960s. The council has flagged these as high-cost to service, requiring focused investment for safety compliance in communal areas. Major works budget for 2025/26 includes £1.8m for windows and doors, £3.0m for roof repairs, and £1.7m for heating.
findings.matters: Concentrated aging stock in a single property type increases the risk of capital expenditure spikes and compliance failures. Aging communal areas in flats are high-cost to maintain safely.
findings.figures: 648 flats (23% of stock); majority built 1960s; major works 2025/26 total £14,783,800
findings.quote: the age of these units, mainly constructed in the 1960s, higher cost of servicing these units and maintaining safety standards in communal areas will result in a focus on these homes within the Business Centre Plan and HRA financial provision for the next 5 years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: HRA reserves depleting by 80% over five years — from £36.4m to £7.3m by March 2030
findings.detail: Opening reserves of £36.383m in April 2025 are forecast to decline to £7.251m by March 2030. This rapid depletion leaves minimal financial headroom for income shortfalls, inflation surprises, or urgent capital repairs.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb adverse events or refinance maturing debt. Contingency headroom is critical in housing finance given long asset lives and income volatility.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £36,383,000 (April 2025); closing year 5 £7,251,000 (March 2030); decline £29,132,000 (80%)
findings.quote: Anticipated Reserves of 31 March 2025 £36,383,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: Debt repayment deferred to year 8 (2032/33) — interest-only payments continue while cash constraints persist
findings.detail: Rather than starting loan repayment on schedule, the council defers principal payments until 2032/33. This was forced by the rent reduction and caps from 2016 onwards, which consumed cash that would have serviced debt. Even then, repayment starts at only £250,000 per annum.
findings.matters: Extended interest-only payments increase total cost of borrowing and narrow the window for principal repayment. This represents refinancing risk and suggests limited financial flexibility for additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Repayment deferred 8 years; £250k pa from 2032/33; increases to £5m (year 14), £7.5m (year 16), £10m (year 23 onwards)
findings.quote: It was anticipated that the HRA would start setting aside sums of money from rent to repay its borrowings when they became due however the introduction of the Welfare Reform and Work Act 2016 rent reduction and the subsequent rent cap at 2.8% below inflation for 2023/24 has reduced the funds available for debt repayment other than 1-4-1 receipts

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: Void rate elevated due to contractor performance issues, reducing current rental income
findings.detail: The council is experiencing higher-than-target void rates 'as a result of performance issues with the void contract.' The plan assumes this will improve to 1.75% from 2027 onwards, with annual void rent loss at that rate estimated at £395,000.
findings.matters: Void properties generate zero rent. Elevated void rates represent near-term cash flow headwind from a controllable operational issue (contractor performance).
findings.figures: Current void rate 1.7%; Target 1.75% from 2027/28; Annual void rent loss at target rate £395,000
findings.quote: the Business Plan incorporates an assumption for a void rate of 1.75% from 2027 onwards after a higher rate initially as a result of performance issues with the void contract.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: Historic rent reduction of £50 million leaves 30-year business plan significantly underfunded
findings.detail: The Welfare Reform and Work Act 2016 imposed a mandatory 1% annual rent reduction for four years. This permanent loss of £50m in anticipated rental income strikes at the financial foundation of the 2011 settlement, under which the council took on £103.3m of debt.
findings.matters: The original debt settlement relied on rental income of £491.96m over 30 years. The £50m loss (10% of planned income) weakens the business case for the entire £103.3m refinancing and leaves less room for future shocks.
findings.figures: £50,000,000 income loss; Original settlement payment £103,292,000; Expected 30-year income £491,964,000
findings.quote: the Welfare Reform and Work Act 2016 imposed a rent reduction in the social sector of 1% per annum for 4 years which has significantly reduced the anticipated income over the period (£50,000,000).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: MHCLG issued Best Value Notice in December 2023 over excessive borrowing and debt levels
findings.detail: Although the notice was removed after one year, MHCLG instructed the council to 'continue leading its own improvement journey and taking steps to reduce and manage its overall debt.' This signals regulatory concern about debt sustainability.
findings.matters: Regulatory intervention on borrowing is a governance red flag. Lenders need clarity on the debt reduction trajectory and the council's ability to deliver improvement.
findings.figures: £100m HRA debt; Best Value Notice issued December 2023
findings.quote: the receipt of the non-statutory Best Value Notice in December 2023 focused on the Council's overall borrowing levels and despite the notice having been removed on its anniversary by MHCLG, they stated that 'we expect the council to continue leading its own improvement journey and taking steps to reduce and manage its overall debt'.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: Housing development target missed by 90% — only 13 of 125 planned units delivered by 2026
findings.detail: The council aimed to deliver 125 additional homes by 2026 to align with Local Plan aspirations for 145 new council homes. To date, only 13 properties have been acquired. Site scarcity and escalating land and building costs are blocking progress.
findings.matters: Development failure means forgone rental income from new units and raises questions about capital deployment and management capability against stated strategic objectives.
findings.figures: 125 units targeted by 2026; 13 delivered (10% delivery rate); Local Plan aspiration 145 additional homes
findings.quote: The Asset Management Plan aims to have an approved programme of delivery of 125 additional units by 2026, the scarcity of sites and escalating land and building costs has resulted in only 13 properties being acquired to date.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1Housing Revenue Account Business Plan Review 2025 Version 2
findings.headline: Benefit dependency at 70% and rising, with direct UC payments creating rental income collection risk
findings.detail: Benefit-dependent tenants have risen from 54% in April 2019 to 70% by April 2025. Payment of housing benefit directly to tenants under Universal Credit creates cash flow uncertainty. The document explicitly flags this as a risk to rental income.
findings.matters: Rental income is the primary source for debt service. Escalating benefit dependency, especially with direct UC payments bypassing the landlord, threatens the reliability of this income stream.
findings.figures: 70% of tenants on UC or HB (April 2025); 54% in April 2019; 1,971 tenants on benefits
findings.quote: The number of tenants in receipt of benefit has increased over 4 years by 10%, with 70% of tenants now receiving Universal Credit or Housing Benefit (54% in April 2019). This increase and the payment of the housing element of Universal Credit direct to tenants may impact on rental income as the roll out of the new system continues.

news_drafts.headline: Strategic asset disposal programme following prior debt warning from MHCLG
news_drafts.lead: Prior regulatory flagging for high debt followed by forced asset sales indicates the council was pushed to address debt levels and is shedding assets to restore financial stability.

news_drafts.headline: Quarterly vacancy loss of £603,848 with multiple assets unlet
news_drafts.lead: Prolonged vacancies reduce revenue whilst the council continues to carry debt servicing and holding costs, eroding returns and income certainty.

news_drafts.headline: Portfolio heavily concentrated in office sector experiencing sharp value declines
news_drafts.lead: Concentrated exposure to a declining asset class increases portfolio risk and limits income resilience if office sector conditions deteriorate further.
